source_text: Venio nunc ad ordinarias sententias eius, per quas proprietatem doctrinae suae inducit, ad edictum, ut ita dixerim, Christi: beati mendici, — sic enim exigit interpretatio uocabuli, quod in Graeco est — quoniam illorum est dei regnum. iam hoc ipsum, quod a benedictionibus coepit, creatoris est, qui uniuersa, prout edidit, nulla alia uoce quam benedictionis dedicauit: eructauit, inquit, cor meum sermonem optimum. hic erit sermo optimus, benedictionis scilicet, qui et noui quoque testamenti initiator agnoscitur de ueteris exemplo. quid ergo mirum, si et ab adfectibus creatoris ingressus est per huiusmodi dictionem, semper mendicos et pauperes et hnmiles ac uiduas et pupillos usque diligentis consolantis adserentis uindicantis, ut hanc Christi quasi priuatam benignitatem riuulum credas de fontibus saluatoris? reuera quo dirigam nescio in tanta frequentia eiusmodi uocum, tamquam in silua uel in prato uel in nemore pomorum. passim prout incidit res petenda est. inclamat psalmus: iudicate pupillo et mendico et humilem et pauperem iuste tractate, liberate pauperem et mendicum de manu peccatoris eruite. item psalmus septuagesimus primus: iustitia iudicabit mendicos populi et faciet saluos filios pauperum, et in sequentibus de Christo: omnes nationes seruient ei, — Dauid autem uni genti Iudaicae praefuit, ne qui in Dauid putet dictum, quia et ille susceperat humiles et necessitatibus laborantes — quod liberauerit, inquit, a dynasta mendicum; parcet mendico et pauperi et animas pauperum saluas faciet, ex usura et iniustitia redimet eorum animas, et honoratum nomen eorum in conspectu ipsius. item: auertantur peccatores in inferosomnes nationes, quae dei obliuiscuntur, quoniam non in finem obliuioni habebitur mendicus: tolerantia pauperum non peribit in finem. item: quis sicut deus noster, qui habitat in excelsis et humilia prospectat in caelo et in terra, qui suscitat mendicum de terra et de stercore exaltat pauperem, uti sedere eum faciat cum principibus populi, utique in regno suo? sic et retro in Basiliis Anna, mater Samuhelis, spiritu gloriam deo reddens: qui, inquit, excitat pauperem de terra et (de stercore eleuat) mendicum, uti sedere eum faciat cum dynastis populi et in thronis gloriae, utique regalibus. per Esaiam uero quomodo inuehitur in uexatores egenorum! uos autem, ad quid incendistis uineam meam et rapina mendici in domibus uestris?
pass_a_gloss: I come now to the ordinary opinions of him, through which he introduces the property of his doctrine, to the edict, so to speak, of Christ: blessed are the beggars, — for thus the interpretation of the word demands, which in Greek is — because the kingdom of God is of theirs. already this itself, which he began from blessings, is of the Creator, who, as he gave forth all things, dedicated them with no other voice than that of blessing: my heart, he says, has uttered an optimal word. this will be the optimal word, clearly of blessing, which is also recognized as the initiator of the new testament from the example of the old. what therefore is surprising, if also from the affections of the Creator he began through this kind of diction, always comforting, championing, and vindicating the beggars and the poor and the humble and the widows and the orphans, so that you might believe this kindness of Christ to be a stream from the fountains of the Savior? indeed, I do not know where to direct myself in such a great frequency of such words, as if in a forest or in a meadow or in a grove of fruits. everywhere, as the matter falls, it is to be sought. the psalm cries out: judge the orphan and the beggar and treat the humble and the poor justly, free the poor and the beggar from the hand of the sinner, rescue. likewise the seventy-first psalm: justice will judge the beggars of the people and will make the sons of the poor safe, and in the following concerning Christ: all nations will serve him, — but David was in charge of one nation, the Jewish, lest anyone think it was said about David, because he also had taken up the humble and those laboring in necessities — what he says, he will free the beggar from the powerful one; he will spare the beggar and the poor and will save the lives of the poor, from usury and injustice he will redeem their lives, and their name will be honored in his sight. likewise: the sinners will be turned away into hell, all nations that forget God, because the beggar will not be given over to oblivion in the end: the patience of the poor will not perish in the end. likewise: who is like our God, who inhabits the heights and looks upon the humble in heaven and on earth, who raises the beggar from the earth and from the dung heap exalts the poor, so that he makes him sit with the princes of the people, certainly in his kingdom? so also earlier in the song of Hannah, the mother of Samuel, giving glory to God in spirit: who, she says, raises the poor from the earth and lifts the beggar from the dung heap, so that he makes him sit with the rulers of the people and on the thrones of glory, certainly royal. but through Isaiah, how he inveighs against the oppressors of the poor! you, however, why have you set my vineyard on fire and the plunder of the beggar in your houses?

pass_b_english: I now turn to his standard proof-texts, the ones he uses to establish his doctrine's character — in effect, Christ's own edict: 'Blessed are the beggars,' for that is what the Greek word demands — 'because the kingdom of God belongs to them.' (Luke 6:20) The very fact that he opens with blessings marks this as the Creator's work; when he brought everything into existence, he consecrated it with nothing but the voice of blessing: 'My heart has uttered a noble word.' (Psalm 45:1) That noble word is precisely a word of blessing, and it is recognized as the New Testament's foundation precisely because it follows the Old Testament's pattern. So why be surprised if he also grounds his teaching in the Creator's own affections, consistently comforting, championing, and vindicating beggars, the poor, the humble, widows, and orphans — as though Christ's peculiar kindness were a mere rivulet flowing from the Savior's own springs? Honestly, I hardly know where to look in this dense thicket of such language; it is like wandering through a forest, a meadow, or an orchard. The material lies scattered everywhere, to be gathered as it falls.

The Psalm cries out: 'Give justice to the orphan and the beggar; treat the humble and the poor fairly. Rescue the poor and the beggar from the hand of the wicked.' (Psalm 82:3-4) Likewise Psalm 71: 'Justice will judge the beggars of the people and save the children of the poor,' and a few verses later, speaking of Christ: 'All nations will serve him' — David ruled only the single Jewish nation, so no one should imagine the prophecy refers to David, even though he too lifted up the humble and those crushed by need — 'he will free the beggar from the oppressor; he will spare the beggar and the poor and save the lives of the poor; from usury and injustice he will redeem their lives, and their name will be honored in his sight.' (Psalm 72:12-14) Again: 'The wicked shall return to Sheol, all nations that forget God, for the beggar will not be forgotten forever; the patience of the poor will not perish in the end.' (Psalm 9:17-18) Again: 'Who is like the Lord our God, who dwells on high yet looks down on the humble in heaven and on earth? He raises the beggar from the dust and lifts the poor from the ash heap, to seat them with princes — with the princes of his people — in his kingdom.' (Psalm 113:5-8) So also, earlier, in the song of Hannah, Samuel's mother, giving glory to God in the Spirit: 'He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the beggar from the ash heap, to seat them with nobles and make them inherit a throne of glory.' (1 Samuel 2:8) But through Isaiah, how he thunders against the oppressors of the poor! 'What do you mean by burning my vineyard? The plunder of the beggar is in your houses.' (Isaiah 3:14)

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass A provides a literal gloss, while Pass B provides a fluent translation with necessary scripture citations (Luke 6:20, Psalm 45:1, Psalm 82:3-4, Psalm 72:12-14, Psalm 9:17-18, Psalm 113:5-8, 1 Samuel 2:8, Isaiah 3:14) which correspond to the quoted/alluded content in the Latin. All clauses, including the complex descriptions of the Creator's voice and the various Psalms, are preserved.
